Toronto Youth, Ward by Ward

Youth programs and services in each of Toronto’s 25 wards — who pays, who runs them — set against need: young people living there, children in low income, and Neighbourhood Improvement Areas, the places the City targets for extra investment.

November 2026 · Councillors elected for 2026–2030 · 2,668 listings, each with a source: 539 City-paid · 655 City-run · 1,092 Ontario & Canada · 382 charities & other groups. 2,154 in a ward; 514 citywide.

Introduction

What this record is

This is a ward-by-ward record of what Toronto has for its young people — the programs, places and grants in each of the city’s 25 wards. It was compiled in November 2026, for the council elected for 2026–2030, so that anyone can see, ward by ward, what is there and where the gaps are. What it shows is what is published: if a program is missing from the record, that means no published source for it was found — not proof that it does not exist.

Every listing in the record has a published source. There are 2,668 listings, each counted once in one of four groups: 539 funded by the City, 655 delivered by the City, 1,092 funded by Ontario or Canada, and 382 privately funded. Of these, 2,154 are listed under a ward and 514 are listed as citywide.

City funding in the record comes to about $88.8 million in published grant awards from the City’s 539 City-funded listings, 2022 to 2026. That is grant money only: it does not include the cost of running City-delivered services, or money from Ontario, Canada or charities. About $85 million of it is tied to a ward, and about $3.9 million across 76 citywide listings. One $35,000 grant to the Jean Augustine Centre in Ward 3 (Etobicoke—Lakeshore) was published by the City twice in 2024 — in the Black-Mandated Funding Framework Established stream list and in the Innovation 2024 list. It appears twice in the record, but its dollars are counted once, in the ward-tied total. About $85 million plus about $3.9 million comes to about $88.9 million, while the total is about $88.8 million — the small gap is rounding.

Listings are shown alongside need in each ward: children in low income — 14.7% of children aged 0 to 17 in the City of Toronto, 67,725 of 461,810, from the 2021 Census and 2020 incomes, a pandemic year, counted on the after-tax low-income measure. Each ward page also shows how many young people aged 5 to 24 live in the ward, and the City’s Neighbourhood Improvement Areas, the neighbourhoods the City has marked for extra investment.

One pattern stands out in Scarborough. Its six wards hold 440 of the 2,154 listings tied to a ward — about 1 in 5. Counted on the same basis as the money, they hold 117 of the 463 City-funded listings tied to a ward — about 1 in 4 — but only $7.2 million of about $85 million in City funding tied to a ward — about 1 in 12. Those shares alone say nothing about funding against need, and the citywide funding also reaches young people in Scarborough; the ward pages show the need in each ward.

The money is not spread evenly even within Scarborough. Scarborough Centre (Ward 21) holds about $3.0 million in City funding across 29 City-funded listings — about $104,000 each. Scarborough North (Ward 23) holds $22,155 across 7 City-funded listings — about $3,000 each — the second-lowest total dollars of any ward; the lowest is Ward 2, Etobicoke Centre, at $17,500. The gap is driven mainly by grant size, not by the number of listings.

There is also a gap in what anyone can prove. Only 423 of the 1,616 listings the record started with publish any results — 26%. The other 1,052 listings were added in November 2026 and have not been through that check yet — for outcomes, not for sources: every listing has a published source. The record notes that most of what the 423 publish is a count of people served, not evidence of change.

How to read this record. Each ward page stands on its own, for the councillor and staff of that ward. The dollar figures are published dollars only — a minimum, not the full amount spent, because not every dollar is published. City awards run 2022 to 2026, and 2026 is a partial year; the year for each listing is printed beside it on the ward pages, where a year is published. The comparisons here describe where the published money sits. They are not a league table, and they are not a verdict on any ward.

    What’s missing

    What’s missing — and why

    2,668 listings: 539 City-paid, 655 City-run, 1,092 Ontario & Canada, 382 charities & other groups — 2,154 in a ward, 514 citywide. A listing counts only where a published source supports it; where a program is real but no public record names it, it appears here instead — never estimated. One limit: City grant lists don’t say who serves youth, so City-paid listings are those identifiable as youth-serving by name or mandate. A gap is called “no data” only where the data genuinely isn’t published.

    Checked

    How sure are we?

    • Source lists re-add to their printed totals. The City’s 2025 Community Safety & Partnership list matches its printed $20,602,184.97 to the cent; 2024 and 2023 match exactly too.
    • Every placement checked against the map. Each listing rests on a published source and was checked by computer against the City’s official ward boundaries. Listings with uncertain status say so on the card — two West Scarborough sites no longer on the club’s current locations page, and SKETCH, a historical record for an organization that closed in 2025. A spot check re-verified 10 of 10 placed listings against their addresses.
    • Every listing checked. Category and ward confirmed against its source: 26 ward corrections in all — 19 from checking all 1,209 listings with an address against the City’s ward map. Not a sample.
    • The counts re-add. 539 + 655 + 1,092 + 382 = 2,668 listings; ward names and councillors on all 2,154 ward listings match the official 2026 list with zero mismatches.
    • Independent check passed. A reviewer who didn’t build this record re-ran the totals and ward corrections, plus a fresh sample of 40 listings (40 of 40 agreed).
    • Doubts are printed on the cards. 39 listings carry a note — source-list duplicates, a closed organization, operators, sites no longer on a current locations page. Nothing uncertain was quietly removed.

    What each listing carries — and how often it’s published

    The 1,616 listings in the original record were checked for the same extra facts: what it does, ages served, youth reached, cost per young person, how often it runs, cost to families. Unpublished facts simply don’t show. Newest listings (November 2026) not yet checked. Program details found for 1,615 of 1,616; who it’s for, 1,613.

    Youth served published · 390 of 1,616 · 24%
    Youth served, with its basis (reported, target or registered) and year — 390 of 1,616 Ages served — 57% How often it runs — 53% Cost to families — 46%

    Cost per young person shows only where money and people share one basis — 122 listings; for 59 more it was deliberately not computed. Behind these rates: Trillium states a people count in only 8 of 275 grant descriptions; sports clubs publish no registration counts; the newest published recreation waitlist figure is from 2016.

    Read first

    Before you use these numbers

    • City funding after 2024 is only partly published. See gaps 6 and 7 above.
    • A City-paid group’s ward is its mailing address. For City-funded groups, the ward is the mailing address the City prints in its grant lists. The City’s own footnote (report 2024.EC17.3, Appendix 5): “Wards represent the mailing address of the applicant group. Project service locations vary considerably.” City-run places are placed by real address.
    • Ontario & Canada funders publish no delivery address — recipient and city only. How the 1,092 listings were placed is under “How sure are we” above.
    • YESS money is multi-year. Full agreement values spanning 2020–2028 ($203.2M total) — not one year’s spending. Labelled everywhere; never added to other totals.
    • Charities & other groups: best effort, not complete. No complete public list exists. Only verifiable programs counted; each ward page rates the checking (strong, moderate, thin). “Thin” = little verified, not nothing there.
    • Nobody has checked whether money matches need. No independent review has tested it. The Auditor General’s 2013 review covered process, not where money landed.
    • Ward low-income rates are estimates; dollar totals add years. The City publishes one rate — 14.7% (2021 Census, 2020 incomes); ward rates are worked out from published counts and marked as estimates. Totals combine years: City awards 2022–2026; Trillium values fiscal 2021–2026. Years are printed beside every total.
    Method

    How this was counted

    • Two tests sort every listing. “Run by” = who operates it; “Paid for / Funded by” = who pays. One program can sit under different kinds for different funding records.
    • Duplicates, handled openly. A grant the City printed twice counts as printed (one Unison grant appears twice in the City’s list); a grant in two City streams shows in both, dollars counted once; two federal agreements for one program count once.
    • Counts are listings. Each program, place or grant counts once, whatever its size. Counts compare how much is listed — not how big each thing is.
    Sources: City of Toronto Community Funding Unit grant lists (2024.EC17.3 App. 5; 2023.EC7.3 Apps. B & 3; 2025 Community Funding App. 3) and its 2024 Impact Report; Ontario Trillium Foundation grant data, fiscal 2021–2026; Canada Summer Jobs lists (2024–2026) and federal YESS agreement disclosures; United Way Greater Toronto disbursements; Toronto Open Data (2021 Census Ward Profiles; Neighbourhood Improvement Areas; facilities; ward boundaries); Toronto Public Library; Wellbeing Toronto directories, checked against current sources. Every ward listing links to its source. Councillors: City Clerk’s official 2026 election results.
